chapters.title: Chapter 2: How to Actually Buy and Sell Unlisted Shares in India

lessons.title: Red Flags and Scams: Why Liquidity Is the Core Risk

children.text: Three weeks after wiring the money, Meena checks her demat account and sees it: 500 shares of the logistics startup, credited exactly as promised, matching the signed SPA and the Form SH-4 she kept a copy of. She did everything right. She feels like she has finally cracked unlisted investing. Then, a week later, she gets a call from someone claiming to represent a well-known dealer platform, telling her she has been allotted a "bonus allocation" of extra shares in a hot pre-IPO company, and that she needs to pay a ₹12,000 "SEBI compliance and processing fee" to release it.

body.text: Every check in this chapter protects you from being cheated. None of them protects you from illiquidity itself, the risk that you simply cannot sell when you want to, even in a completely honest deal. That risk never goes away, and it is worth understanding on its own terms.

children.text: The Scam Catalogue: Patterns to Recognise Instantly

Almost every scam in the Indian unlisted-share market is a variation on a small number of recognisable patterns. Learning to spot the pattern matters more than memorising any one story, because the specific company name, the specific dealer, and the specific number will always change.

body.caption: Recognisable scam patterns in the unlisted-share market

cells: You are asked to pay a "compliance fee", "escrow charge" or "GST" upfront before shares or a "bonus allocation" are released
Legitimate transfers never require the buyer to pay a fee just to "unlock" a deal; real costs like stamp duty are small, fixed, and paid as part of the transfer itself
The seller has no shares to actually deliver, or has already sold the same block to someone else through an informal PoA arrangement
The seller cannot show a demat statement or company/RTA confirmation of their own holding before you pay
Fake documents shown to simulate an imminent, credible IPO
The "DRHP" cannot be found on SEBI's own public filings; only the seller's copy exists
Promises of a specific, guaranteed return or listing price
No legitimate market participant can guarantee where a stock will list or trade, since that is set by public demand on listing day
A fake website or lookalike domain mimics a real, reputable dealer platform
Small URL differences, and requests to pay into a personal account instead of the platform's own verified account
Coordinated posts hype an unlisted stock as the "next big pre-IPO opportunity", creating urgency to buy from the promoter's own inventory
Anonymous tipsters, screenshots of "gains", pressure to decide within hours

body.text: If you remember only one thing from this catalogue, remember this: a genuine guarantee of returns or listing gains does not exist in this market. Nobody, however well-connected, can honestly promise you a specific outcome for an unlisted company's future listing. The word "guaranteed" is, on its own, close to conclusive proof that something is wrong.

children.text: Why All of These Work: The Illiquidity Multiplier

These patterns succeed for a structural reason, not just because victims are careless. A listed stock's price is public, continuous, and checkable in seconds on any trading app. An unlisted share has none of that. There is no ticker to glance at, no independent quote to compare a dealer's price against, and no exchange where a fabricated claim would be caught within moments. The same absence of a continuous public market that makes staying private attractive to founders, covered earlier in this course, also gives a scammer far more room to operate before a victim can catch the deception.

body.label: Why scams thrive here
body.value: No continuous public price to check against
body.context: Unlike an NSE-listed stock, whose price you can verify in seconds via any trading app, there is nothing to instantly cross-check an unlisted-share quote against, which is exactly what makes an inflated or fabricated quote hard to catch quickly.

children.text: Fraud Risk vs Illiquidity Risk: Two Different Problems

It helps to separate two problems that get lumped together as "unlisted shares are risky". Fraud risk is about being deliberately deceived: fake shares, a seller double-selling the same block, a fabricated document. Illiquidity risk is different, and present even when nobody is lying to you at all: you may simply be unable to find a buyer when you want to sell, or only at a price far below what you think is fair, because there is no exchange guaranteeing you one. Every checklist so far in this chapter has been about the first problem. The rest of this lesson is about the second.

columns.label: Fraud Risk
points: Caused by deliberate deception: fake shares, double-selling, fabricated documents
Protected against through verification: SPA, Form SH-4, demat credit checks, DRHP checks
Can, in principle, be reduced to near zero with enough diligence

columns.label: Illiquidity Risk
points: Present even in a completely honest, fully documented transaction
Protected against through position sizing and time horizon, not verification
Cannot be eliminated, only managed, since there is no exchange to sell into on demand
The subject of the rest of this lesson

children.text: What Illiquidity Actually Costs You, Even When Nothing Goes Wrong

Suppose Meena's deal was completely honest in every respect, which it was. If she now wants to sell before any IPO, she cannot place a sell order and get a market price the way she could with a listed stock on an app like Zerodha. She has to find a specific buyer herself, or through a dealer, and negotiate one-on-one. A buyer who knows Meena needs to sell, rather than wants to, has every incentive to offer less than any theoretical "fair value", precisely because she has no other venue to sell into. This gap between what a share might be theoretically worth and what a motivated seller can actually get in a hurry is the illiquidity discount, and it exists even when every document is genuine and every party is honest.

body.title: Quick Check: Stamp Duty on a Share Transfer
body.prompt: Meena buys 500 unlisted shares at ₹500 each through a Form SH-4 transfer. Share transfer stamp duty is 0.25% of the transaction value. What is the stamp duty payable, in rupees?
body.explanation: Transaction value = 500 × ₹500 = ₹2,50,000. Stamp duty at 0.25% = ₹625. This is one of the few genuinely fixed, small costs in an otherwise unpredictable unlisted-share deal, which is exactly why any "processing fee" running into thousands of rupees should stand out as abnormal.

children.text: Since illiquidity cannot be verified away the way fraud risk can, it needs a different answer entirely: sizing. Treat unlisted and pre-IPO holdings as the most illiquid, highest-risk sleeve of a portfolio, not a core holding, and never commit money you might need access to within a defined horizon. Spreading a commitment across several companies and vintages, whether done directly or through a pooled AIF or PMS vehicle covered earlier in this chapter, also reduces how much a single bad outcome can hurt.

stats.label: Suggested max allocation to unlisted/pre-IPO bets
stats.value: A small, single-digit % of net worth
stats.context: A common rule of thumb among wealth advisers for genuinely illiquid, high-risk private holdings

stats.label: Minimum realistic holding horizon
stats.context: Given how long companies now stay private, as covered earlier in this course

stats.label: Companies for meaningful diversification
stats.context: Spreading single-company risk, whether done directly or via a pooled AIF/PMS vehicle

body.title: The Absolute Walk-Away List
steps: Any request to pay a fee, "compliance charge" or "GST" before shares or documents are released
Any promise of a guaranteed return, guaranteed listing gain, or guaranteed listing date
A seller who cannot show proof of their own holding, such as a demat statement, before you pay
Pressure to decide or pay within hours, especially through anonymous social media or Telegram tips
A "DRHP" or "SEBI approval" that cannot be independently verified on SEBI's own public website

body.title: The "Bonus Allocation" Call
body.scenario: A caller claiming to represent a well-known dealer platform tells Meena she has been allotted a "bonus allocation" of additional shares in a hot pre-IPO company, but must first pay a ₹12,000 "SEBI compliance and processing fee" to release it.
body.prompt: Using everything covered across this chapter, how should Meena respond?
body.modelAnswer: This is a textbook advance-fee pattern, and it fails on multiple counts at once. She never applied for any "bonus allocation", which is itself a warning sign. No legitimate share transfer requires the buyer to pay a fee to release shares they are supposed to already own; the real, small costs in a transfer, like stamp duty on Form SH-4, are paid as part of the transfer itself, not as a separate upfront charge to "unlock" something. And "SEBI compliance fee" is not a real category of payment SEBI charges retail investors directly for a private transaction. The correct response is to not pay anything, independently contact the platform through its verified official channels rather than the number that called her to confirm whether this is genuine, and treat the unsolicited nature of the call itself as the biggest red flag.

body.title: The Single Most Reliable Tell
body.question: Which of these is the single most reliable sign of a scam in the unlisted-share market?
options: A dealer platform with a professional-looking website
A price that is close to the company's last known funding round valuation
A promise of a guaranteed return or guaranteed listing gain
A seller who insists on a signed Share Purchase Agreement before payment
body.explanation: Nothing in unlisted-market investing can be genuinely guaranteed, since there is no exchange and no certainty about if or when a listing happens or what price it fetches. A guarantee is, by itself, close to proof that whatever is being promised cannot be honestly true. Insisting on a signed SPA, by contrast, is a sign of a legitimate deal, not a scam.

body.title: Red Flags and Illiquidity: Key Terms

cards.definition: A fraud pattern where a victim is asked to pay a fee upfront to "release" or "unlock" funds, shares or an allocation that does not actually exist.
The reduction in price a seller often must accept to find a buyer quickly in a market with no continuous public price or guaranteed buyer, such as the unlisted-share market.
The risk of being deliberately deceived, through fake shares, double-selling, or fabricated documents. Reduced through verification and documentation.
The risk of being unable to sell an investment when you want to, at a fair price, even in a completely honest transaction. Managed through position sizing and time horizon, not verification.

points: Most scams in the unlisted-share market follow a handful of recognisable patterns: advance-fee requests, non-existent or already-sold shares, fabricated DRHPs, guaranteed-return promises, platform impersonation, and social-media pump schemes.
A guaranteed return or guaranteed listing gain is, by itself, the single most reliable sign that an offer is not genuine, since nothing in this market can honestly be guaranteed.
These scams work partly because the unlisted market has no continuous public price to check claims against, unlike a listed stock you can verify in seconds.

Fraud risk (being deceived) and illiquidity risk (being unable to exit even in an honest deal) are different problems. Verification and documentation address the first; position sizing and time horizon address the second.

Illiquidity cannot be verified away. Treat unlisted-share investing as a small, deliberately sized sleeve of a portfolio, with money you can genuinely afford to have locked up for years, not a core holding.
Never pay a fee to "release" shares, documents, or an allocation you did not apply for. Legitimate transfer costs, like stamp duty, are small, fixed, and paid as part of the transfer itself.

body.text: This lesson is for education only and is not investment or legal advice. Meena is fictional and used purely for illustration. Position-sizing and allocation figures shown are general rules of thumb, not personalised financial advice, and should be discussed with a qualified financial adviser given your own circumstances. Stamp duty rates and other costs cited are illustrative and should be independently verified before any real transaction.
